questions.question: In an M/G/1 queue, $S_r(t)$ is the time the job in service at time $t$ still needs, with $S_r(t)=0$ when the server is idle. Why does the time average $\mathbb{E}[S_r]$ depend on the second moment $\mathbb{E}[S^2]$ and not only on $\mathbb{E}[S]$?
options: Jobs waiting in the queue add their own squared service times to $S_r(t)$, so the queue brings in $\mathbb{E}[S^2]$.
During a service of length $S_k$, $S_r$ falls linearly from $S_k$ to $0$, so each service adds an area $S_k^2/2$.
Poisson arrivals make $S_r(t)$ exponential whatever $S$ is, and an exponential has second moment $2(\mathbb{E}[S])^2$.
$S_r$ stays equal to $S_k$ throughout a service of length $S_k$, so each service adds a rectangle of area $S_k^2$.

questions.question: In an M/G/1 queue with load $\rho=\lambda\mathbb{E}[S]<1$, the time-average remaining service time is $\mathbb{E}[S_r]=\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{1}{t}\int_0^t S_r(s)\,\mathrm{d}s$, where $S_r(s)$ is what the job in service at time $s$ still needs. How do idle periods of the server enter this average?
options: They count with $S_r=0$, so $\mathbb{E}[S_r]=\rho\,\mathbb{E}[S_r\mid S_r>0]$.
They are left out, so $\mathbb{E}[S_r]$ is the mean remaining time of a busy server.
They count with $S_r=\mathbb{E}[S]$, the full service the next arriving job will need.
Idle periods fill a fraction $\rho$ of the time, so $\mathbb{E}[S_r]=(1-\rho)\,\mathbb{E}[S_r\mid S_r>0]$.

questions.question: In an M/G/1 queue with mean service time $\mathbb{E}[S]$ and $\mathbb{E}[S^2]<\infty$, for which service times is the mean remaining service time of a busy server, $\mathbb{E}[S_r\mid S_r>0]$, equal to $\mathbb{E}[S]/2$?
options: For every service distribution, since an arrival lands uniformly within the service in progress.
For exponential services, since memorylessness makes the remaining part half a fresh service.
For deterministic services only, since with $\operatorname{Var}(S)=0$ there are no long services to be hit more often than short ones.
For any service distribution symmetric about its mean, since long and short deviations cancel.

questions.question: In an M/G/1 queue the service times are exponential with mean $\mathbb{E}[S]$. What is the mean remaining service time $\mathbb{E}[S_r\mid S_r>0]$ of the job in service, as seen by an arrival that finds the server busy, and why?
options: $\mathbb{E}[S]/2$, because on average the arrival finds the current service half finished.
$2\mathbb{E}[S]$, because arrivals land in services whose mean length is twice $\mathbb{E}[S]$.
$\rho\,\mathbb{E}[S]$, because the server is busy only a fraction $\rho$ of the time.
$\mathbb{E}[S]$, because by memorylessness the rest of the service is again exponential.

questions.question: In a single-server queue, which quantity is the remaining service time $S_r(t)$ at time $t$?
options: The total work still to be done at time $t$ for all jobs present, in service or waiting.
The time the job in service at $t$ still needs, and $0$ when the server is idle at $t$.
The service time the job in service at $t$ has already received since its service began.
The full service time $S_k$ of the job in service at $t$, and $0$ when the server is idle.

questions.question: Jobs arrive at an M/G/1 queue as a Poisson process with rate $\lambda=0.2$ per minute; service times have $\mathbb{E}[S]=2$ minutes and $\operatorname{Var}(S)=3$ square minutes, so $\rho=0.4$. What is the time-average remaining service time $\mathbb{E}[S_r]$?
options: $0.3$ minute
$0.4$ minute
$0.7$ minute
$1.4$ minutes

questions.question: An M/G/1 workstation has load $\rho=0.6$, mean service time $\mathbb{E}[S]=5$ minutes and squared coefficient of variation $C_s^2=\operatorname{Var}(S)/(\mathbb{E}[S])^2=0.5$. What is the time-average remaining service time $\mathbb{E}[S_r]$?
options: $0.75$ minute
$3.75$ minutes
$11.25$ minutes
$2.25$ minutes

questions.question: In an M/G/1 queue with arrival rate $\lambda=0.2$ per minute, service times are uniform on $[0,6]$ minutes, so $\mathbb{E}[S]=3$, $\mathbb{E}[S^2]=12$ and $\rho=0.6$. What is the mean remaining service time $\mathbb{E}[S_r\mid S_r>0]$ seen by an arrival that finds the server busy?
options: $2$ minutes
$1.5$ minutes
$3$ minutes
$1.2$ minutes

questions.question: In a $200$-minute observation window a single server is idle at both ends and serves $40$ jobs; their service times sum to $80$ minutes and their squares sum to $300$ square minutes. What is the time average of the remaining service time $S_r$ over the window?
options: $1.5$ minutes
$0.75$ minute
$1.875$ minutes
$3.75$ minutes

questions.question: An M/M/1 queue has arrival rate $\lambda=0.4$ per minute and exponential service times with mean $\mathbb{E}[S]=2$ minutes. What is the time-average remaining service time $\mathbb{E}[S_r]$?
options: $0.8$ minute
$2$ minutes
$1.6$ minutes
$3.2$ minutes

questions.question: In an M/G/1 queue the arrival rate $\lambda$ and mean service time $\mathbb{E}[S]$ stay fixed, with $\rho<1$, while $\operatorname{Var}(S)$ is raised from $v>0$ to $v+\Delta$ with $\Delta>0$. How does the time-average remaining service time $\mathbb{E}[S_r]$ change?
options: It stays the same, because the load $\rho=\lambda\mathbb{E}[S]$ does not change.
It is multiplied by $(v+\Delta)/v$, because $\mathbb{E}[S_r]$ is proportional to $\operatorname{Var}(S)$.
It decreases, because more variable service means more short jobs, which most arrivals meet.
It increases by exactly $\lambda\Delta/2$, whatever the starting variance $v$ is.

questions.question: In an M/G/1 FIFO queue with $\rho<1$ and $C_s^2=3$, a student estimates the mean waiting time in queue by $\mathbb{E}[L]\,\mathbb{E}[S]$, as if each of the $\mathbb{E}[L]$ jobs an arrival finds, including the one in service, needed a full mean service time. How does this estimate compare with the true $\mathbb{E}[W]$?
options: It is too small: the job in service still needs $2\mathbb{E}[S]$ on average, not $\mathbb{E}[S]$.
It is too large: the job in service is on average half done and needs only $\mathbb{E}[S]/2$.
It is exact: by PASTA the arrival finds $\mathbb{E}[L]$ jobs, each needing $\mathbb{E}[S]$ on average.
It is too large: with high variability most jobs found in service are short ones.

questions.question: The proof that $\mathbb{E}[S_r]=\frac{\lambda}{2}\mathbb{E}[S^2]$ in the M/G/1 queue first uses the renewal reward theorem with reward $S_k^2/2$ per departure, giving $\mathbb{E}[S_r]=\delta\,\mathbb{E}[S^2]/2$ with departure rate $\delta$. Which assumption allows $\delta$ to be replaced by $\lambda$?
options: Poisson arrivals, since PASTA makes the departure rate equal to the arrival rate.
The finite second moment, since $\mathbb{E}[S^2]<\infty$ keeps the mean reward per departure finite.
Rate stability, since in the long run jobs then leave the system as fast as they arrive.
Independent service times, since averages of $S_k^2$ then converge to $\mathbb{E}[S^2]$.

questions.question: Jobs arrive at an M/G/1 FIFO queue as a Poisson process at rate $\lambda=0.3$ per hour; service times have $\mathbb{E}[S]=2$ hours and $C_s^2=3$, so $\rho=0.6$. What is the mean waiting time in queue $\mathbb{E}[W]$?
options: $2.4$ hours
$6$ hours
$4$ hours
$3$ hours

questions.question: A single server is idle at time $0$. Job 1 arrives at time $0$ with service time $3$; job 2 arrives at time $1$ with service time $1$ and waits until job 1 is done. What is the time average over $[0,10]$ of the remaining service time $S_r(t)$ of the job in service?

In an M/G/1 queue with arrival rate $\lambda=0.25$ per minute, half of the jobs need $1$ minute of service and the other half need $5$ minutes, so $\mathbb{E}[S]=3$ and $\rho=0.75$. Among arriving jobs that find the server busy, what fraction find a $5$-minute job in service?

A single-server queue has i.i.d. service times with $\mathbb{E}[S^2]<\infty$ and is rate stable with arrival rate $\lambda$, but its arrivals do not form a Poisson process. Which statement about the remaining service time $S_r$ is correct?
options: Both its time average and the mean seen by arriving jobs equal $\frac{\lambda}{2}\mathbb{E}[S^2]$, since rate stability makes arrivals see time averages.
Neither its time average nor the mean seen by arriving jobs need equal $\frac{\lambda}{2}\mathbb{E}[S^2]$, since the renewal reward step needs Poisson arrivals.
Its time average still equals $\frac{\lambda}{2}\mathbb{E}[S^2]$, but the mean seen by arriving jobs can differ from it, since only the PASTA step needs Poisson arrivals.
Arriving jobs still see a mean of $\frac{\lambda}{2}\mathbb{E}[S^2]$ by the area argument, while the long-run time average may be different.

questions.question: An M/G/1 queue has arrival rate $\lambda=0.5$ per minute and service times with $\mathbb{E}[S]=1$ minute but $\mathbb{E}[S^2]=\infty$, so $\rho=0.5$. Which statement about its remaining service time $S_r$ and mean waiting time in queue $\mathbb{E}[W]$ is correct?
options: The queue is not rate stable, because stability needs $\mathbb{E}[S^2]<\infty$ as well as $\rho<1$.
$\mathbb{E}[S_r]=\rho\,\mathbb{E}[S]=0.5$ minute, because at load $\rho<1$ only the mean service time matters.
$\mathbb{E}[S_r]\le\mathbb{E}[S]=1$ minute, because a remaining service can never exceed a full service.
The time average of $S_r$ is infinite, so $\mathbb{E}[W]$ is infinite even though $\rho<1$.

questions.question: A single-server queue with Poisson arrivals at rate $\lambda=0.5$ per minute has i.i.d. service times with $\mathbb{E}[S]=4$ minutes and $\operatorname{Var}(S)=4$ square minutes, so $\rho=2$; no jobs are blocked. What is the long-run time average of the remaining service time $S_r$?
options: $5$ minutes
$2.5$ minutes
$2$ minutes
It grows without bound

questions.question: Jobs arrive at a single machine as a Poisson process at rate $\lambda=0.2$ per minute. Machine A serves every job in exactly $3$ minutes; machine B needs $1$ minute with probability $0.75$ and $7$ minutes with probability $0.25$, so $\mathbb{E}[S]=2.5$. Which machine gives the smaller $\mathbb{E}[S_r]$, and what are the two values?
options: Machine A: $0.9$ minute for A against $1.3$ minutes for B.
Machine B: $0.625$ minute for B against $0.9$ minute for A.
Machine B: $1.25$ minutes for B against $1.5$ minutes for A.
Machine A, whose deterministic service gives $\mathbb{E}[S_r]=0$, against $0.675$ minute for B.
